semin-durr:1-1.t:
His saying: {تَبَّتْ يَدَآ أَبِي لَهَبٍ}: i.e. they have lost. The explanation of this root was given in Sūrat Ghāfir at His saying: {إِلاَّ فِي تَبَابٍ} [Ghāfir: 37]. The verb was attributed to the two hands figuratively, because most acts are performed with them, even though the whole of the one cursed is meant. His saying «تَبَّتْ» is an imprecation (duʿāʾ), and «تَبَّ» is a statement, i.e. what was invoked against him has occurred; as in the poet's saying:
4668 - جَزاني جَزاه اللَّهُ شرَّ جَزائِه ... جزاءَ الكِلابِ العاوياتِ وقد فَعَلْ
(He repaid me — may Allah repay him the worst of repayment — with the repayment of howling dogs; and He has done so.)
This is supported by the reading of ʿAbd Allāh [ibn Masʿūd]: «وقد تَبَّ». The apparent view is that both are imprecations; and in this there is something resembling the general coming after the specific, because the two hands are a part — even though the literal hands are not meant; He only expressed it with the two hands because acts are mostly performed with them.
The generality read «لَهَبٍ» with fatḥa on the hāʾ, and Ibn Kathīr with sukūn on it [«لَهْبٍ»]. It was said: they are two dialect forms with one meaning, like al-nahr and al-nahar, al-shaʿr and al-shaʿar, al-nafar and al-nafr, al-ḍajar and al-ḍajr. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is a case of altering proper names, like his saying 'Shums ibn Mālik' with ḍamma" — meaning that the origin is Shams, with fatḥa on the shīn, which was altered to ḍamma; and he is alluding to the poet's saying:
4669 - وإنِّي لَمُهْدٍ مِنْ ثَنَائِي فَقاصِدٌ بِهِ ... لابنِ عَمِّ الصِّدْقِ شُمْسِ بنِ مالكِ
(I am presenting some of my praise, directing it to the true cousin, Shums ibn Mālik.)
The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] allowed that «شُمْس» may be transferred from «شُمْس», the plural [of shamūs, restive], from the saying: "the tails of restive (shums) horses"; so it would not be a case of alteration at all. He was given this kunya either because of the flaming of his cheeks — he was bright-faced and ruddy — or because of what he will come to, the flame of Hell, as in their saying "Abū al-Khayr" and "Abū al-Sharr" because [good or evil] issue from them; or because the kunya is more prevalent than the name; or because it is lesser than it — hence He mentioned the prophets by their names, not their kunyas; or because of the ugliness of his name, for his name was "ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā", so He turned to the kunya. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: why did He call him by his kunya, when the kunya is an honour?" — then he mentioned three answers: either because he was well known by his kunya, or because of the ugliness of his name as stated, or because his destination is the flame of Hell — end of quote. This implies that the kunya is nobler and more complete, not lesser, which is the opposite of a view stated just above.
It was read: «يدا أبو لَهَبٍ», with the wāw in the place of the genitive. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "As was said: ʿAlī ibn Abū Ṭālib and Muʿāwiya ibn Abū Sufyān, so that nothing in it is changed and it becomes confusing to the hearer. Flīta ibn Qāsim, the emir of Mecca, had two sons, one of them ʿAbdi-llāh with the genitive and the other ʿAbda-llāh with the accusative." The readers did not differ concerning His saying {ذاتَ لَهَب}: it is with fatḥa. The difference is that it is a verse-ending (fāṣila), and if it were made quiescent, the correspondence [of the verse-endings] would be lost.

semin-durr:2-2.t:
His saying: {مَآ أغنى}: «ما» may be negative or interrogative. On the second it is in the position of the accusative by what follows it, the implied form being: "What did wealth avail?" It was placed first because it has the right to the beginning of the clause.
His saying: {وَمَا كَسَبَ}: «ما» here may be in the sense of «الذي», with the referring pronoun omitted; or maṣdariyya, i.e. "and his earning"; or interrogative, meaning: "and what did he earn?", i.e. he earned nothing — the Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said this, making the interrogative mean negation. On this basis it may be negative, the meaning being as he mentioned; but this is not apparent. ʿAbd Allāh [ibn Masʿūd] read: «وما اكْتَسَبَ».

semin-durr:3-3.t: His saying: {سيصلى}: the generality read with fatḥa on the yāʾ, sukūn on the ṣād and the lām without shadda, i.e. he himself will burn. Abū Ḥaywa, Ibn Miqsam and ʿAbbās in his preferred reading (ikhtiyār) read with ḍamma, fatḥa and shadda [«سَيُصَلَّى»]. Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read with ḍamma and sukūn [«سَيُصْلَى»].

semin-durr:4-4.t:
His saying: {وامرأته حَمَّالَةَ الحطب}: the reading of the generality is in the nominative, taking them as a clause of mubtadaʾ (subject) and khabar (predicate) brought to state that. It was also said: «وامرأتُه» is conjoined to the pronoun in «سَيَصْلى», which is made permissible by the separation with the object. On this view there are several views about «حَمَّالةُ الحطبِ»: that it is a naʿt (adjective) of «امرأتهُ» — that being permissible because the annexation is genuine (ḥaqīqiyya), since the past is meant; or that it is ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition); or that it is a badal (substitute), because it is close to non-derived nouns owing to the pure [definiteness of its] annexation; or that it is the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, i.e. "she is the carrier". Ibn ʿAbbās read «ومُرَيَّتُهُ» and «ومُرَيْئَتُهُ» in the diminutive, except that he kept the hamza at one time, and at another changed it into yāʾ and assimilated [the yāʾ] into it.
The generality read {حَمَّالَةُ} in the nominative, and ʿĀṣim in the accusative. It was said: by way of reviling (shatm); "he did a fine thing (jamīl) who reviled Umm Jamīl" — al-Zamakhsharī said this; she was known by the kunya Umm Jamīl. It was also said: it is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «امرأتُه», if we make it nominative by conjunction to the pronoun. Making it a ḥāl from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase after it, if we make that the khabar of «امرأتُه», is weak according to the majority, because it precedes its abstract governor (al-ʿāmil al-maʿnawī). Some found the ḥāl reading problematic because of what was said before, that the past is meant by it, so it becomes definite through the annexation; so how can it be a ḥāl according to the majority? Then he answered that the future is meant, because it is reported in the exegesis that she will carry on the Day of Resurrection a bundle of the firewood of the Fire, as she used to carry firewood in this world.
Concerning His saying {حَمَّالَةَ الحطب} there are two views. The first: it is literal. The second: it is a figure for going about with slander and sowing discord among people. The poet said:
4670 - إنَّ بني الأَدْرَمِ حَمَّالو الحَطَبْ ... هُمُ الوشاةُ في الرِّضا وفي الغضبْ
(The Banū al-Adram are carriers of firewood: they are the slanderers in content and in anger.)
Another said:
4671 - مِنْ البِيْضِ لم تُصْطَدْ على ظَهْرِ لأْمَةٍ ... ولم تَمْشِ بين الحَيِِّ بالحطبِ الرَّطْبِ
(One of the fair women, not caught upon a disgrace, and who does not go about among the clan with fresh firewood.)
He made it fresh to point to its smoking, and this is close to reinforcing the metaphor (tarshīḥ al-majāz). Abū Qilāba read {حاملةَ الحطبِ} on the pattern fāʿila; it admits [the same senses as] the reading of the generality. ʿAbbās read «حَمَّالةٌ للحطَبِ» with tanwīn and the object made genitive by a redundant (zāʾida) lām strengthening the governor, as in His saying, exalted is He: {فَعَّالٌ لِّمَا يُرِيدُ} [Hūd: 107]. Abū ʿAmr, in one transmission, read «وامرأتُه» with the hāʾ snatched (ikhtilās), without full lengthening.

semin-durr:5-5.t:
His saying: {فِي جِيدِهَا حَبْلٌ}: «في جيدِها» may be the khabar (predicate) of «امرأتُه», with «حبلٌ» as its fāʿil (agent); or a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «امرأتُه» on the view that it is an agent [conjoined to the pronoun], with «حبلٌ» likewise nominative by it; or a fronted khabar with «حَبْلٌ» a postponed mubtadaʾ (subject), the clause being a ḥāl or a second khabar. Al-jīd: the neck; its plural is ajyād. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
4672 - وجِيْدٍ كجِيْدِ الرِّئْمِ ليس بفاحِشٍ ... إذا هي نَصَّتْهُ ولا بمُعْطَّلِ
(And a neck like the neck of a white antelope, not ungainly when she raises it, nor bare of ornament.)
{مِّن مَّسَدٍ} is an adjective of «حَبْل». Al-masad: the fibre of the doum palm; it was also said: fibre in general; and it was said: it is the bark of a tree in Yemen. Al-Nābigha said:
4673 - مَقْذُوْفَةٌ بِدَخِيْسِ النَّحْضِ بَازِلُها ... له صريفٌ صَريفُ القَعْوِ بالمَسَدِ
(Pelted with compact flesh, her tusk grinds with a creak like the creak of a pulley-wheel on a palm-fibre rope.)
It may also be of camels' hides and hair; he recited:
4647 - ومَسَدٍ أُمِرَّ مِنْ أَيانِقِ ...
(And a rope twisted firmly from [the hides of] young she-camels…)
[Translator's note: the verse number appears thus (4647) in the source; by sequence 4674 would be expected.]
One says: "a man mamsūd of build", i.e. strong of it.
